opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the starting point is a simple observation. We've been scaling these large models by feeding them more and more data, mostly text and images scraped from the internet. And there's a growing sense that we're approaching the limits of that. High-quality human-generated data is finite, and a lot of what's being produced now is itself generated by models, which brings its own problems.

At the same time, there's this enormous resource sitting around that we mostly ignore: the trained models themselves. Think about Hugging Face. There are hundreds of thousands, now well over a million, models uploaded. Each was trained on some dataset, with significant compute, and the weights encode what the model learned. In a sense, the weights are a compressed representation of the data and the training process. Yet once a model is trained and published, we use it for inference or fine-tune it, and that's it. We never treat the population of models as a dataset.

That's what my group has been working on. We call it learning on model weights, or hyper-representations. You take a model zoo, a large collection of trained networks, and treat each network's weights as a data point. Then you train a model on that, for example a self-supervised autoencoder or transformer that learns a latent space of neural networks. Once you have that, interesting things become possible. You can predict properties of a model like accuracy or generalization gap just by looking at its weights, without running it on any data. And you can go generative: sample new weights from the learned distribution to initialize or even directly produce models that perform well, sometimes better than random initialization or standard pretraining.

So why is this valuable as data runs short? First, it's knowledge already distilled. Somebody paid the compute cost to compress a dataset into those weights. If we can learn across many models, we're in some sense learning from all the data those models saw, without needing the raw data. That matters for privacy and licensing too, since often you can't share the data but you can share the model.

Second, it's a different modality with its own structure. Weights have symmetries, like permutation symmetries in neurons, and once you account for those, there's a surprisingly rich, learnable structure. The model population isn't random; it lives on some manifold, and learning that manifold tells you something fundamental about how networks learn.

And third, it's a growing resource. While fresh human data may plateau, the number of trained models keeps exploding. Every company, every lab, every hobbyist is producing checkpoints. So if we develop the methods to learn from weights at scale, we tap into a data source that grows with the field itself.

Of course, there are big challenges: scaling to really large models with billions of parameters, handling heterogeneous architectures, and dealing with those symmetries properly. But I think of it as a shift from learning only from data to also learning from models. That's a pretty exciting direction for where the next generation of foundation models might come from.

r001.rationale: The response links data shortages to learning from models, but does not describe a shift toward learning at test time.

r002.rationale: It says trained weights encode what models learned and that learning across them reuses knowledge for which others already paid the compute cost.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about for a while now, and it really started with a very simple observation. We've spent the last decade or so training an enormous number of neural networks. If you go to Hugging Face, you have hundreds of thousands of models sitting there, in every architecture, trained on every kind of task, by all sorts of people. And the question I kept asking myself is: what do we actually do with all of these? Mostly, we use them for inference, maybe we fine-tune them, and that's it. But if you step back, every one of these weight sets is the result of a lot of compute, a lot of data, and a lot of human decisions about hyperparameters, data curation, architecture, and so on. All of that is encoded in the weights. So to me, the weights themselves are a kind of artifact that we have been systematically ignoring as a data modality.

Now, why does that matter in the context of data running short? We've seen the scaling laws, we know that performance keeps improving with more data and more compute, and we also know that the high-quality text on the internet is finite. There are estimates that we're going to hit the wall on usable, non-synthetic data fairly soon, if we haven't already in some domains. So people are looking at synthetic data, they're looking at curation, and so on. My argument is that there's another pool we haven't tapped, and that's the population of already-trained models.

If you think of a model's weights as a compressed representation of the training data and the training process, then a population of models is, in a sense, a dataset of learned functions. And you can learn from that. In our group we've been working on what we call model zoos, where we train thousands of small models with controlled variations, and then we treat the weights as the input to another learning problem. You can learn to predict properties of a model just from its weights: accuracy, how it was trained, how robust it is. But more interestingly, you can learn a representation of the weight space itself, and then you can sample from it. You can generate new models, or at least new initializations, that already sit in a good region of the loss landscape.

That's where it connects to the data problem. Training a large model from scratch is expensive partly because you start from a random point and you have to burn an enormous amount of data to get anywhere reasonable. If instead you could start from a point that was informed by everything we've already learned about what good weights look like, you'd need fewer samples, fewer steps, to reach the same quality. So the existing weights become a prior. They're not a replacement for data, but they're a way of extracting value from data that has already been consumed. Somebody already paid the price of training on that data; the knowledge is sitting there in the parameters, and right now we throw most of that away every time we start a new run.

There's also a sustainability angle to this, which I care about. The amount of carbon and energy we put into training runs that are then partially duplicated by the next lab is huge. Treating weights as reusable, learnable data is one path toward not redoing that work over and over.

The honest caveat is that this is still a young area. Most of the convincing results are on small models, where you can afford to train a population of thousands. Scaling that idea up to very large models is an open question, because you can't train thousands of them. But I think the direction is right, and I think over the next few years we'll see the community start to treat weight space as a first-class data modality rather than just an output.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using existing weights as a prior to reduce data and training steps, but does not attribute a shift toward learning at test time to data shortages.

r002.rationale: It says existing weights encode prior compute and data, and reusing them extracts value from work already paid for instead of repeating it.

astra-6.text:
Well, if you think about it, every trained model has already absorbed information from the data it was trained on. And we spend a tremendous amount of computation getting that information into the weights. Usually, we then treat those weights as the endpoint: we deploy the model and use it for inference. But they can also be a starting point for learning something new.

That becomes particularly interesting when access to more training data is constrained. There are many existing models, trained on different tasks and different datasets, and their weights encode some of what they learned. Can we reuse that knowledge, combine it, or learn across a collection of models, rather than always going back to the original data and training from scratch?

Of course, weights aren’t interchangeable with data, and you can’t simply average arbitrary models together and expect a better model. Understanding how to extract and transfer that knowledge is the research challenge. But the opportunity is to make use of an accumulated investment in data and computation that we otherwise leave largely untapped.

r001.rationale: The response links constrained training data to reusing existing models, but it does not describe a shift toward learning at test time.

r002.rationale: It says model weights encode learned knowledge and can be a starting point for new learning, reusing the computation already spent training those models.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you look at how we train models today, we put a tremendous amount of data, compute, and energy into a training run, and the result is a set of weights. Those weights encode something about the data the model has seen and the task it has learned. So the question is: can we reuse that accumulated knowledge more directly, instead of always starting again from the original data?

And we have this growing population of trained models. They’ve learned different tasks, on different datasets, with different architectures. I see that as another source of information that we haven’t fully tapped into. You can think of an individual model as a data point, and then ask what we can learn across a collection of models.

Of course, weights aren’t just interchangeable—you have to deal with how networks represent information and with symmetries between them. But if we can learn useful representations of those weights, we may be able to transfer knowledge, construct better initializations, or combine capabilities. As access to fresh training data becomes more constrained, that makes the knowledge already captured in models a very interesting resource.

r001.rationale: The response says fresh training data is becoming constrained, but it does not identify a shift toward learning at test time.

r002.rationale: It describes trained models’ weights as embodying accumulated data and compute, then presents reusing knowledge in those weights as a way to transfer knowledge and improve initializations.
